Better public data sources include: Secretary of State business entity registrations (LLC and corporation filings show PM company names and registered agents), city/county business license registries (PM companies register for local business licenses), and rental property databases (some counties maintain rental registration programs requiring PM company disclosure). Engineering lift is moderate-to-high: aggregate state real estate licensing databases where PM licensing exists, scrape Secretary of State business entity databases filtering for "property management" in business name, parse city business license registries, cross-reference rental registration programs in jurisdictions requiring PM company disclosure (e.g., NYC rental registration, California city rental housing programs), enrich with business directory lookups (Google Business, YellowPages, Yelp commercial property managers), geocode addresses, classify by property type focus (residential/commercial/mixed), normalize portfolio size estimates based on employee count or online unit listings, deduplicate multi-state operators. Score not higher than 7 due to: (a) fragmented public data sources (PM licensing varies by state, requiring aggregation across licensing boards, business registries, and local business licenses rather than single federal database), (b) moderate-to-high engineering complexity to compile comprehensive national dataset from multiple state and local sources, (c) existing HOA/community association brief (2026-05-15) covers overlapping segment (some PM companies manage HOAs), though property management companies represent distinct broader market beyond HOAs (residential rental buildings, commercial properties, corporate housing), and (d) data completeness challenges in states without PM-specific licensing (must rely on business name pattern matching and business registry scraping rather than clean regulatory database).

data_wanted: State real estate licensing boards in states requiring property management companies or property managers to hold real estate broker or salesperson licenses (California Department of Real Estate maintains public license lookup for property managers requiring DRE broker license, Texas Real Estate Commission TREC requires PM company brokers to be licensed, Florida DBPR real estate license search, New York Department of State real estate licensee search, Illinois IDFPR, Colorado DORA real estate division) — license databases contain business name, DBA, principal broker name and license number, business address, phone, email (where provided), license status, license issue/expiration dates. Secretary of State business entity registrations: Search state corporation and LLC databases filtering for "property management" in legal business name or DBA (e.g., "ABC Property Management LLC", "XYZ PM Inc.") across all 50 states — business entity filings are public records containing legal name, business address, registered agent, entity type, filing date, status (active, dissolved, suspended). City and county business license registries: Many jurisdictions require PM companies to obtain local business licenses — scrape city business license databases (searchable online in larger cities) for property management category or business name pattern matching. Rental property registration programs: Some cities and counties mandate rental property registration disclosing property management company name and contact (e.g., New York City HPD rental registration, California cities with rental housing programs, college town rental registration ordinances) — public databases link rental addresses to managing PM companies. Industry association member directories: National Association of Residential Property Managers (NARPM.org) member directory, Institute of Real Estate Management (IREM.org) Certified Property Manager designees, local apartment association member lists (publicly searchable directories showing PM company members). Business directory enrichment: Google Business listings for "property management" by city (scrape business name, address, phone, website, review count indicating active operation), Yelp commercial category for property management, Better Business Bureau accredited PM companies, YellowPages property managers category. Target fields per PM company record: Company legal name and DBA, owner/principal name(s), property manager names (where disclosed in licensing), business mailing address, physical office location(s), phone number, email address (where public or scraped from website contact pages), website URL, state real estate license number (in licensing states), business entity type (LLC, corporation, sole proprietorship), property types managed via categorization (residential single-family, multifamily apartments, commercial office, retail centers, industrial warehouses, mixed-use, HOA/condo association management, student housing, senior living/assisted living, hospitality short-term rentals, self-storage facilities), approximate portfolio size in units managed (where publicly stated on website or estimated from employee count and online unit listings), number of office locations, geographic markets served, year established, membership in professional associations (NARPM, IREM, local apartment associations), and state(s) of operation. Classify PM companies into size buckets: micro (1-50 units managed, often individual landlords self-managing or small startups), small (51-500 units, local independent PM firms), medium (501-2,000 units, regional PM companies with multiple markets), large (2,001-10,000 units, institutional-grade regional operators), and enterprise (10,000+ units, national PM platforms like Greystar, Lincoln Property Company, FPI Management, though largest may self-develop software rather than buy). Target all active PM companies across residential, commercial, and mixed-use sectors. Approximately 270,000-350,000 total PM companies in US: breakdown includes 200,000-250,000 residential PM firms (single-family rental managers, multifamily apartment operators, HOA/condo managers), 30,000-50,000 commercial PM companies (office buildings, retail centers, industrial property), 20,000-30,000 specialized sectors (student housing, senior living, self-storage, hospitality), and 10,000-20,000 mixed-use managers. Target output: 300,000-400,000 rows (includes branch offices and multi-location operators appearing as separate records per location to enable regional targeting). Data is partially public: PM licensing databases are public records in states requiring licenses (CA, TX, FL, NY represent 40%+ of US rental market), Secretary of State business registries are public in all states, city business licenses are often searchable online, rental registration programs publish PM company names as public records, and business directory listings (Google Business, Yelp) are publicly scrapable — however no single centralized federal database exists, requiring multi-source aggregation and normalization to achieve national coverage.
